To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the volume of the left ventral temporal cortex, which is a key substrate of verbal knowledge, predicts verbal ability in old age, and that the fractional anisotrophy of the arcuate fasculus, which is an important tract for language processing, predicts verbal executive ability in old age.
The volume of the temporal lobe and white matter fractional anisotrophy of the arcuate faciculus predict different aspects of verbal ability in older age.
the brain's white matter (WM), and in particular, the WM tracts that link the brain's language areas, is related to verbal ability in later life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural substrates of human intelligence and the mechanisms that support the development of cognitive skills over the lifespan.
understanding how structural brain measures are associated with verbal ability in older age.
the neurobiological underpinnings of human intelligence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the brain regions that are important to language processing in older adults are those that are involved in semantic memory and language processing, and these are different from those involved in general intelligence.
the brain is a very complex organ, which is not only made of grey and white matter, but also of other components, such as blood vessels, meninges, cerebrospinal fluid, etc.
this research is the first to investigate the grey and white matter correlates of verbal ability traits, in a large sample of older adults.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structural integrity of language networks, in particular the arcuate fascicle, is associated with the executive component of verbal ability.

the brain regions that support verbal abilities are different from those that support non‐verbal abilities, and that the brain regions supporting verbal abilities are more likely to show age‐related changes in the brain than the brain regions that underlie non‐verbal ability.
verbal processing abilities in older age are predicted by the integrity of both grey and white matter brain structures.
The main takeaway from our work is that

verbal abilities in older age can be decomposed into a latent factor that indexes the storage of verbal information and another that indexes executive processes involved in accessing this information in an appropriate manner, with different brain regions contributing to each.
the structural brain correlates of verbal ability are complex and depend on a combination of both GM and WM parameters.
the structural brain correlates of cognitive abilities depend on the specific demands of the task.
